tier_reason: Independent Percona sysbench-tpcc run (author Vadim Tkachenko explicitly uses InnoDB as the baseline) with full hardware/software versions and public scripts, configs and raw results (github.com/Percona-Lab-results/201803-sysbench-tpcc-myrocks). No compiler or build flags are stated (packaged Percona Server 5.7.21-20 binaries), so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Almost 5x higher average tps at a 5GB cache (4205.714 vs 849.0664 tps; the page says MyRocks outperforms InnoDB 'by almost five times'). The lead shrinks as memory grows, and InnoDB overtakes from 60GB (4756.551 vs 4571.163 tps). At 100GB InnoDB is about 1.30x faster (5961.2 vs 4599.143 tps; ratio derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: This is an independent Percona benchmark, not one by Facebook/Meta. The scripts and raw results are public (Percona-Lab-results/201803-sysbench-tpcc-myrocks) and hardware and software versions are fully stated, but there are no compiler or build flags (server-level benchmark on packaged binaries). The engine tested was the MyRocks build shipped in Percona Server 5.7.21-20, not a binary built from the facebook/mysql-5.6 repo. The run used READ-COMMITTED (MyRocks lacks SELECT..FOR UPDATE under REPEATABLE-READ in Percona Server) and no foreign keys. The page reports periodic 1-second throughput drops for MyRocks. The win depends on memory: it holds only while the dataset-to-memory ratio is high, and InnoDB wins at 60GB and above. The repo is archived. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the LICENSE file is MySQL 8.0's GPLv2 with Oracle's additional linking permission (copyleft).

notes: All 11 memory-point averages were checked against the page table, and hardware matches the page's 'Hardware spec' section. The benchmark_url now redirects to https://www.percona.com/blog/a-look-at-myrocks-performance/ (same content). I read the LICENSE file on the fb-mysql-8.0.32 default branch; its last commit (2025-01-27), archived status and 2,574 stars match the record.

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed EuroSys'19 paper comparing Wormhole against LevelDB's skip list, the STX B+-tree, libart ART and Masstree, with the CPU model and full hardware stated. The paper does not state a compiler or flags, and the repo contains only Wormhole's own concbench/stresstest, not the harness that compares against the baselines, so it is not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Up to 8.4x, 4.9x, 4.3x and 6.6x key-lookup throughput vs skip list, B+ tree, ART and Masstree respectively (abstract and conclusion; these are not single-thread figures, and the paper's default is 16 threads). At 16 threads Wormhole beats the best other index by 1.3x-4.2x per keyset. Single-thread on Az1: 1.266 MOPS vs ART's 0.834 MOPS (about 52% higher). At 16 threads: 19.5 MOPS, 43% higher than ART.
corrections.workload: In-memory point lookups with uniformly random search keys on 8 keysets: Amazon review metadata Az1/Az2 (142M keys, avg 40B), MemeTracker URLs 'Url' (192M keys, avg 82B), and synthetic random fixed-length keys K3-K10 (8B-1024B). There is 1-16 thread scaling on Az1, the per-keyset comparisons use 16 threads, and a networked variant ports the indexes to HERD over 100Gb/s InfiniBand. Baselines are thread-unsafe except Masstree.
corrections.baseline: Skip list (extracted from LevelDB), STX B+-tree (fanout 128), Adaptive Radix Tree (libart from GitHub), Masstree (beta release)
corrections.caveats: Evidence is the EuroSys'19 peer-reviewed paper plus the authors' reference implementation. Hardware is fully specified, but the paper gives no compiler or flags. The repo Makefile defaults to clang with -O3 -flto, but that is not tied to the paper's runs. The comparison harness for skip list/B+tree/ART/Masstree is not in the repo, which has only Wormhole's own concbench/stresstest. The 'up to' ratios are best cases across keysets; per-keyset gains over the best competitor are 1.3x-4.2x. The repo has had no commits since April 2022.

notes: All quoted numbers and the hardware were checked against the archived paper PDF. The record wrongly called the up-to ratios single-thread figures and described the data as URL/webpage keys; the single-thread numbers use the Amazon Az1 keyset. Metadata matches: GPL-3.0, not archived or a fork, 86 stars, last commit 2022-04-29.

tier_reason: This is a first-party Tokutek blog post against stock MongoDB v2.2.RC0 indexes. It gives hardware and links a benchmark client, but states no compiler or flags and reports a single end-of-run 'exit velocity' point. A >50x gain with unstated flags is capped at C anyway.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Over 532x 'exit velocity', i.e. the instantaneous insert rate at 3.5M documents: 2.11 inserts/sec for stock MongoDB vs 1,124.36 inserts/sec for MongoDB with Fractal Tree indexes.
corrections.license: GPL-2.0 and AGPL-3.0 per README (GitHub reports AGPL-3.0); locktree and omt portions also Apache-2.0; separate PATENTS file
corrections.caveats: This is a first-party vendor blog post (Tokutek, later acquired by Percona) testing Tokutek's 2012 Fractal-Tree-indexed MongoDB prototype (the TokuMX precursor), not PerconaFT or TokuDB as packaged today. The baseline is stock MongoDB v2.2.RC0 (MMAPv1 B-tree indexes) on 16GB RAM and 4x10K RPM SAS disks. The post gives no cause for the gap, and the record's global-write-lock explanation is not from the source; the 100-entry multikey index outgrowing RAM (random B-tree I/O) is the likelier driver, so the ratio reflects a disk-bound, out-of-memory regime. The 532x is an end-of-run point measurement, not an average. No compiler flags are stated. tokutek.com is dead; the page was recovered via web.archive.org.

notes: All numbers, hardware, OS and MongoDB version match the archived page (posted 2012-11-13 by Tim Callaghan). Metadata matches: 562 stars, not archived or a fork, last commit 2023-11-28, so stale is correct. I only refined the license wording from README/COPYING.* files.
